key_points: The unsigned lead article "The Problems of Cultural Freedom in Asia" (by Prabhakar Padhye) previews the Rangoon Conference on Cultural Freedom in Asia (17-20 February 1955) and argues Asian intellectuals need positive democratic alternatives such as Gandhism, Radical Humanism and Buddhist Socialism, not just anti-communist polemic, to counter communism's appeal.

A "Notes" column praises Nehru's Indian Science Congress address for defending scientists' independence, treats the Djilas-Dedijer Yugoslav trials as a tragic curdling of decentralisation into orthodoxy, dismisses Rajagopalachari's call for unilateral US nuclear disarmament as naive, and relates Mrinalini Sarabhai's account of restricted freedoms on a dance tour of East Germany.

A news report names India's six-member delegation to the Rangoon conference (Jayaprakash Narayan, M. R. Masani, Asoka Mehta, Eric da Costa, Ram Singh, Laxmanshastri Joshi) with Prabhakar Padhye serving as General Secretary.

Karl A. Wittfogel's centrepiece essay, "The Historical Position of Communist China: Doctrine and Reality," draws on suppressed Marx and Lenin writings on "Oriental despotism" to argue Communist China is not a proto-socialist society but a new form of "general (state) slavery" run by a monopoly managerial bureaucracy.

Nissim Ezekiel announces the launch of Quest, a new bi-monthly arts-and-ideas journal sponsored by the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom, intended to complement Freedom First with a more ambitious literary and cultural mandate.

A "C.C.F. News" column reports on Congress for Cultural Freedom activities worldwide, including an Ernst Reuter memorial lecture series in Berlin and a Preuves meeting in Paris where Andrzej Panufnik and Czeslaw Milosz testified on artistic repression in Communist Poland.

Four book reviews cover U Nu's Burma Under the Japanese (V.B.K.), Celina Lu Zanne's Heritage of Buddha (Madan Lal Sharma), Rorty and Decter's McCarthy and the Communists (Faiz Noorani), and R. N. Carew Hunt's Marxism: Past and Present (Gopal Krishna).

Letters to the editor debate the Committee's anti-communist orientation, with J. K. Kotewal defending continued vigilance and J. Dubashi disputing a prior article's Soviet real-wages statistics, met by an editorial correction of a units error.
The closing 'With Many Voices' page collects topical quotations from Rajagopalachari, Stalin, Vinoba Bhave, S. Radhakrishnan and others on Soviet planning costs and Cold War politics.

U Ba Nyunt, Mayor of Rangoon, opens the Conference on Cultural Freedom in Asia with an inaugural address, "Culture And Freedom," arguing culture cannot flourish without freedom and warning the Welfare State's expansion of planning risks becoming 'a new form of imperialism.'

An unsigned report on the Rangoon conference lists thirty-five delegates from twelve countries and records M. R. Masani's argument that co-existence may be possible between states but not between the cultures of democracy and communism, alongside Jayaprakash Narayan's keynote on Bhoodan as voluntary social action.

Messages of support to the conference from Lin Yutang, Sir Arthur Wijeyewardhene, Kotaro Tanaka, Han Suyin and Bertrand Russell are reproduced, urging the Congress for Cultural Freedom to remain free of party affiliation and stressing Asia's spiritual traditions.

A 'Notes' column reads Malenkov's fall and Bulganin's rise as evidence Khrushchev has had to placate army interests, praises a 150-signatory Telugu writers' declaration for parliamentary democracy, and satirises a new 'United Marxist Party' in Bombay for claiming independence from Moscow while remaining pro-Soviet.

S. S. Vasan, President of the Film Federation of India, argues in a reproduced speech, "Problems Of The Indian Cinema," that Indian cinema's slow artistic progress owes to low economic standards and mass tastes, and proposes reforms including reduced admission tax and liberalised censorship.

Yatin Gaznavi's essay-review of Jacques Maritain's Man and the State argues political conflict lies less in competing lists of rights than in the hierarchy of values by which they are ordered, while explicitly dissenting from Maritain's claim that only the Church can handle 'matters of intelligence.'

Three reviews cover R. P. Masani's Education for World Understanding (Adam Adil), Tadeusz Wittlin's Reluctant Traveller in Russia on two years in Soviet forced-labour camps (Laeeq Futehally), and a Czechoslovak Industries Exhibition in Bombay.

I.C.C.F. News reports a Calcutta send-off tea party for delegates departing to Rangoon and a Poona Group lecture series on Maharashtra's nineteenth-century reform trends, covering Agarkar, Shinde and Phuley.

'With Many Voices' closes with press quotations including Clement Attlee comparing Russian foreign policy to Tsarist imperialism and Sir John Kotelawala crediting America's atom bomb with keeping 'free Asia' free of war.

Prof. Hannan Ezekiel's lead essay, "The Dangers Of Physical Planning," warns that P. C. Mahalanobis's 'physical planning' model for the Second Five Year Plan carries an inherently totalitarian tendency, citing D. R. Gadgil's fear that the National Sample Survey could 'exterminate all parallel agencies.'

Sir John Latham, President of the Australian Committee for Cultural Freedom, argues in "The Free Spirit Of Man" that tolerance of opposing opinion is essential to progress, since any regime claiming infallibility treats dissent as heresy leading to labour camps and liquidation.

A 'Notes' section welcomes Congress's defeat of the Communist Party in the Andhra elections despite the Communists retaining 31.6% of the vote, reports Sir Mirza Ismail's speech on communist infiltration, and rebukes New Statesman editor Kingsley Martin for saying he would have voted communist in Andhra.

An unsigned report on a British Ministry of Defence booklet, "Communist China And Prisoners Of War," documents the mistreatment and 're-education' of 978 British POWs held by Communist China during the Korean War, noting only 40 were judged genuine converts.

Martin S. Dworkin's "George Orwell On The Screen," reprinted from the New Leader, criticises the Halas and Batchelor animated film of Orwell's Animal Farm for its Disney-influenced style and 'heavy' narration, judging it more effective propaganda for Europeans unfamiliar with Soviet history than for readers of the book.

Reviews cover Manes Sperber's novel Journey Without End on Jewish resistance in a doomed Polish village (N.E.), C. Groves Haines's The Threat of Soviet Imperialism featuring George F. Kennan (M.B.S.), and Karl Barth's Against the Stream, whose 'narrow path between Moscow and Rome' the reviewer judges untenable given Soviet capacity for terror.
C.C.F. News previews the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Milan conference on 'The Future of Freedom' (September 1955) and a Paris exhibition of paintings by Indian artist Laxman Pai.

I.C.C.F. News reports the Committee's new Bombay office and a members' meeting at which M. David Rousset described evidence of slave labour camps in Communist China and plans for an Asian tribunal of inquiry.

'With Many Voices' includes Ambedkar's remark comparing the Constitution to a temple now occupied by 'devils' and Salvador de Madariaga's warning that ordinary Russians, not the regime, hold the moral claim on Western sympathy.

The unsigned editorial 'Towards A Communist Pattern?' alleges the Second Five Year Plan's drafting team under Mahalanobis is dominated by Iron Curtain economists, quoting Jayaprakash Narayan's charge that its 'seven authors... are all men from behind the Iron Curtain,' and criticises V. K. R. V. Rao's proposed National Labour Force as a possible precursor to forced labour.

Guy J. Pauker's essay 'Sardar Panikkar -- A Gifted Opportunist,' abridged from World Politics, portrays K. M. Panikkar as an opportunist whose Asia and Western Dominance was written to flatter Asian audiences seeking to accommodate Soviet and Chinese power, quoting Nehru's remark that Panikkar 'will be Communist in Peking and a champion of freedom in Washington.'

Yatim Ghaznavi's essay 'Literature And Belief' argues twentieth-century fiction suffers an 'erosion of the imaginative soil' as science and psychoanalysis annex territory once held by religion, finding even Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh incapable of 'full-blooded doubt.'

Reviews cover Max Beloff's Soviet Policy in the Far East (Aziz Madni), a Ford Foundation report on its India-supported activities (R.H.), and Ignazio Silone's novel A Handful of Blackberries about a disillusioned Italian communist party worker (Laeeq Futehally).
Letters to the editor debate Dr. Kalidas Nag's foreword to a poetry translation and propose forming 'The Friends of Democratic Nations' to counter communist propaganda domestically.

A news report describes Justice U Chan Htoon of Burma's Supreme Court touring Bombay under I.C.C.F. auspices, linking Buddhist revival in Burma, Thailand and Ceylon to resistance against communism and materialism.
C.C.F. News notes the Italian Association for Cultural Freedom's Rome meeting and a Hamburg lecture series including Siegfried Landshut on 'Karl Marx in our Time.'

'With Many Voices' closes with quotations from Lal Bahadur Shastri and Master Tara Singh on communism, alongside the ICCF membership enrolment form and the masthead naming editor V. B. Karnik and printer Prabhakar Padhye.

V. B. Karnik's lead essay 'Bandung: A Step Towards Integration' argues the Bandung Conference of twenty-nine Asian-African nations became an unexpected rebuke of communism despite fears it would become a pro-communist or anti-Western platform, with China under Chou En-lai playing a conciliatory rather than propagandistic role.

A 'Notes' section praises trade unionists who refused Chinese May Day invitations, criticises the Congress Working Committee's move toward stricter film censorship, endorses Vinoba Bhave's and Morarji Desai's calls for education free of state control, and reports the persecution and deportation of Kalmuck Buddhists in the USSR.

Hasan Muhammad Tiro's report on communist infiltration in Indonesia warns that Premier Ali Sastroamidjojo's government has postponed elections while purging anti-communist officers and pardoning 1948 Madiun coup plotters into ministerial posts.

An unsigned piece and a companion account by Edward Hunter, author of Brain-Washing in Red China, describe the communist campaign that forced Dr. Lin Yu-tang to resign as founding Vice-Chancellor of Nanyang University in Singapore, followed by deadly student rioting.

A review signed 'N.E.' praises Maria Yen's The Umbrella Garden for its firsthand, unembellished account of student life in Red China, tracing the arc from benign early discipline to mandatory 'communal living' and government-assigned graduate jobs.

'Bandung: As Others See It' surveys international press reaction, quoting New York Times correspondents Tilman Durdin and Robert Aldon on Krishna Menon's private criticism of Nehru's handling of the conference and Burma's U Nu's quietly effective role.

Letters to the editor cover a Bombay meeting on Muslim political withdrawal since 1947 (Zafar Fatehally) and an idiosyncratic call for Indian disengagement from Asian geopolitics grounded in 'spiritual doctrines' (Raman Desai).
'With Many Voices' closes with Chester Bowles on Asian revolutions being led by frustrated middle-class intellectuals and Arthur Koestler's chastened line that 'we can at best hope for a reprieve.'

The unsigned editorial 'Let There Be No Mistake' defends Freedom First's earlier criticism of the Mahalanobis Plan Frame now that primary documents are available, citing B. C. Roy's and B. R. Shenoy's dissenting notes, and rejects Congress General Secretary Shriman Narayan's charge that the Committee is a capitalist mouthpiece.

Prof. W. Arthur Lewis's reprinted 'A Socialist Economic Policy' argues Britain's inherited socialist tools -- progressive taxation, economic controls, nationalisation -- have reached the limits of their usefulness and calls for redistributing property ownership more broadly instead of further nationalisation.

Prabhakar Padhye's 'Planning For Freedom' questions whether a one-party-dominated legislature can meaningfully approve the Plan rather than merely rubber-stamp it, while welcoming cottage-industry provisions as a decentralising counterweight to heavy industry.

A review signed 'N.E.' of George N. Schuster's Religion Behind the Iron Curtain documents systematic persecution of religion across the Soviet bloc, quoting a condemned man's son's 1952 letter and Cardinal Mindszenty's final scribbled note to his mother.

A statement drafted by Sir John Latham for the Australian Committee for Cultural Freedom on obscene-literature legislation argues censorship is undesirable in principle except for customs control of imports, recommending court prosecution over an administrative Board of Review.
The 'Notes' section covers Soviet-Yugoslav relations, home rule in Tunisia, Chinese payment-in-kind labour policy, and debates over textbook shortages and the English-language question.

The unsigned editorial 'At The Post' announces that this is the last issue of Freedom First published under the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom banner, continuing instead under the Democratic Research Service as the new journal Quest takes over the literary and cultural brief.

A 'Notes' section warns against Great Power deals over Asian nations made without their elected representatives, argues Vietnam-wide elections would be meaningless unless northern voters can freely oppose Ho Chi Minh, and recounts the Kerala 'Tactical Line' controversy over a leaked Communist Party document.

Arthur Koestler's 'The Trail of the Dinosaur -- I,' reprinted from Encounter, charts humanity's growing destructive power against a stagnant moral curve and argues atomic superiority cannot deter limited, camouflaged local aggression.

The unsigned 'Planning And Democracy' takes issue with Nehru's reported remark that democracy's 'structure' might need reconsidering if it obstructs planning, insisting democracy must come first and planning second, only as a means to a better life.

J. G. Tewari's 'The Danger In Indo-China' argues the Nehru-Bulganin declaration's call for prompt Vietnamese elections, without adequate safeguards against a Communist-controlled North holding 13 million people, plays into Communist strategy to conquer the whole country.

Sudhir Hendre reviews Robert St. John's Through Malan's Africa, describing apartheid South Africa's brutal inequality and tracing discriminatory legislation against Natal Indians from an 1892 poll-tax to the 1946 Ghetto Act.

'With Many Voices' closes on N. V. Gadgil's quip linking planning to rising unemployment and a West Bengal Congress leader's statement that a violence-prone party flying 'a foreign flag' has no right to exist in India.

Nissim Ezekiel's 'Our Concern For Africa' argues India's condemnation of colonialism substitutes moral indignation for genuine political understanding, pointing to Indians' own persistent colour consciousness toward Africans living in India.

Zafar Futehally's report previews the Congress for Cultural Freedom's international conference on 'The Future of Freedom' in Milan (12-17 September 1955), naming attendees including Raymond Aron, J. K. Galbraith, Hayek and India's M. R. Masani, B. R. Shenoy and Amlan Dutta.

A 'Notes' section questions arbitrary Indian passport refusals, condemns escalating violence in Morocco and Algeria, argues hartals are increasingly inappropriate against an elected government, reports Jayaprakash Narayan's condemnation of the August 1955 Patna police firings, and honours Goa satyagrahis killed by Portuguese authorities.

Edward Shils's 'Intellectuals And Politicians In America' traces the historical estrangement between American intellectuals and politicians from the Republic's founding through McCarthyism, concluding the episode set back but did not reverse a century-long healing of the rift.

Arthur Koestler's 'The Trail of the Dinosaur -- II' examines the long-term decline of religious faith since the Copernican revolution, warning nuclear and bacteriological weapons will soon decide whether humanity 'goes the way of the dinosaur.'
A letter from Prabhakar Padhye argues bread and freedom form a unity rather than a false dichotomy, pressing Freedom First to recognise 'economic freedom' as integral to its concept of liberty.
I.C.C.F. News reports the opening of the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Asian office in New Delhi, headed by Padhye, and lectures by Kodanda Rao and Edward Shils.

'With Many Voices' quotes Eisenhower on never trading freedom 'for the pottage of a false peace' and communist leader P. Ramamurthi crediting Nehru's foreign policy to Lenin's thesis of peaceful co-existence.

V. B. Karnik's lead essay 'A Tactic Or A New Policy?' weighs whether the post-Stalin Soviet 'thaw' is genuine or tactical, citing the Austrian Treaty and Geneva summit against Khrushchev's own warning that the smile does not mean abandoning Marx and Lenin.

A 'Notes' section welcomes South Vietnam's new republic under Diem, endorses Nehru's sympathetic approach to North-East Frontier tribal peoples while warning of Chinese infiltration, and criticises a proposed National Book Trust as risking political favouritism over private publishing.

M. R. Masani's report on the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Milan conference details debates on planning versus freedom, contested claims about Soviet economic progress, and his own intervention pressing Western delegates on solidarity with underdeveloped countries.

An unsigned report on Indonesia's first general election describes a dangerously fragmented result -- Nationalists, Masjumi, Nahdatul Ulama and Communists near-even -- warning a nationalist-led coalition reliant on communist support could produce a Soviet-satellite 'people's democracy.'

'History In The Making In Soviet Russia' reproduces the 1954 and 1955 Soviet Encyclopedic Dictionary entries on Malenkov side by side, showing his biography cut from 108 to 53 lines after his resignation, and compares the practice to Orwell's 1984.

Reviews cover Philip Spratt's Blowing Up India, tracing his path from Comintern agent implicated in the Meerut Conspiracy case to disillusioned anti-communist writer (Aziz Madni), and Dagobert Runes's The Soviet Impact on Society, arguing communism reproduced capitalism's worst features once implemented (M.B.S.).
'With Many Voices' includes Picasso dismissing Soviet painting as monotonous and militaristic, and Acharya Kripalani's self-description as 'a paralysed socialist.'

V. B. Karnik's lead article 'Let Us Know Who Kisses Us And Why' criticises the Indian government's elaborate, state-orchestrated reception of Bulganin and Khrushchev, objecting to the 'cynical use... of children as instruments of diplomacy' and the Soviet leaders' attacks on Western democracies during their Parliament address.

A 'Notes' section endorses Vinoba Bhave's view that states reorganisation is chiefly administrative, condemns the twelve deaths in police firing during the Samyukta Maharashtra agitation, and disputes Rajkumari Amrit Kaur's claim that China's health services outpace India's.

Bertram D. Wolfe's 'Peaceful Co-Existence' dissects the term as Soviet 'Newspeak' masking simultaneous internal purges and external world conquest, tracing its origins to Trotsky's 1917 peace programme and Lenin's opportunistic use of peace rhetoric.

M. B. Shah's 'Philosophy Of Freedom' traces freedom's historical emergence through liberalism, arguing democracy's failure to realise the Declaration of the Rights of Man in practice fuelled fascism and communism, and calls for a 'positive freedom' via Erich Fromm and M. N. Roy.

W. Z. Laqueur's 'The Double Think And Double Talk,' reprinted from The New Leader, contrasts Bulganin and Khrushchev's public praise of Gandhi with Soviet textbooks that still call him a 'traitor,' tracing Soviet experts' opportunistic reversal on Nehru.
Laeeq Futehally's light essay 'Our New Hobby' wryly observes Bombay's new enthusiasm for Nature excursions to spots like Powai Lake and a boom in domestic gardening.
I.C.C.F. News reports Nicolas Nabokov's November 1955 tour of India and the Committee's Annual General Meeting scheduled for 17-18 December in Bombay.
'With Many Voices' quotes Anthony Eden arguing free elections cannot be held while Germany's communist system must be preserved.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'The Challenge Of The Visit' reads the Bulganin-Khrushchev tour of India and Burma, alongside a Soviet 'Nyet' at Geneva and a hydrogen bomb test, as one calculated Soviet peace offensive that risks blurring the moral distinction between Gandhian Congress values and Bolshevik practice.

Asiaticus's 'China Enters Stalinism' traces escalating Chinese Communist campaigns from 1951 film criticism through the 1955 Hu Feng affair, citing 271,074 arrests and concluding China may eventually exceed Soviet-era terror given its greater backwardness.

An unsigned 'Notes' section urges investigation of an Indian reportedly detained in the Vorkuta labour camp, praises the two Lok Sabha members, N. C. Chatterjee and H. V. Kamath, who alone protested the Soviet visit, and criticises a Bombay High Court ruling that passport denial is non-justiciable.

An unsigned report on the I.C.C.F.'s Third General Meeting (17-18 December 1955) records addresses by Asoka Mehta and Nicolas Nabokov and four resolutions, including disapproval of mobilising schoolchildren during the Soviet visit.

'What Would The Marshal Have Said?' describes the cancelled Bombay Press Guild reception for Bulganin and Khrushchev and a combative Rangoon press exchange challenging the Soviets on Panchashila's applicability to their own satellites.

Philip Spratt reviews Gabriel Almond's The Appeals of Communism, highlighting its finding that Communist propaganda emphasises tactical discipline (94%) far more than ideal 'goal qualities' (6%) in canonical texts.

A report details Nicolas Nabokov's December tour of Madras, Bangalore, Mysore and Bombay, and a reader's letter from S. S. Bankeshwar accuses Nehru of a double standard on US versus Soviet military aid and weapons tests.

V. B. Karnik's editorial 'Where Is India Heading?' uses a Times of India editorial on the Congress Amritsar session to warn that the shift from 'socialistic pattern' to 'socialist structure,' adopted without debate, risks one-party totalitarian drift.

A 'Notes' section rebuts a Blitz allegation that the Democratic Research Service instigated the Samyukta Maharashtra riots, criticises a new Copyright Bill for halving the copyright term to 25 years, and reports Austria's success in expelling the communist-aligned World Federation of Trade Unions from Vienna.

Bertram D. Wolfe's essay on the post-Stalin 'collective leadership' of Khrushchev, Bulganin, Malenkov, Molotov and Beria argues the Soviet system's lack of any legitimate succession mechanism makes collective rule an inherently unstable interregnum.
Alex Atkinson's satirical mock travel-brochure 'Come To Sunny Russia,' reprinted from Punch, lampoons Soviet tourism propaganda against the real drabness and surveillance of Moscow life.

An item on the PEN International controversy quotes President Charles Morgan's 1955 questions about whether a Soviet PEN centre could ever be genuinely free of state control, and his refusal to admit writers who are 'instruments of tyranny.'

Reviews cover Sister Cecilia, an escaped Slovak nun's memoir of Czechoslovak communist persecution (A.A.), the launch of the new magazine The Ambassador edited by Sudhir Hendre, and Walter Lippmann's The Public Philosophy, which the reviewer connects to the Indian idea of raja dharma.
I.C.C.F. News reports a Martha Graham seminar, a lecture by Prof. W. S. Woytinsky on the world economy, and a reception for four visiting Japanese women writers.

The unsigned editorial 'Stalin: A Vindication' marks the third anniversary of Stalin's death, arguing the Soviet leadership's own denunciation of Stalin vindicates the journal's earlier criticism while naming Khrushchev, Bulganin, Mikoyan and Molotov as his willing accomplices.

V. B. Karnik's 'Wait And Watch' argues the 20th CPSU Congress rejected Stalinism while retaining Leninism, counselling a cautious middle path between naive trust and reflexive dismissal of Soviet reform.

Franz Borkenau's 'How Mao Bluffed Dulles,' from the New Leader, argues the 1955 Formosa crisis was a deliberate bluff to mask Mao's internal 'Second Revolution' of agrarian collectivisation, and predicts China will deal with Russia and the West on near-equal terms within a decade.
Richard Mowrer's 'The Soviet Woos Franco Spain' documents Soviet efforts since 1954 to court Franco's Spain via prisoner releases and trade, aiming to detach Spain from US economic dependence.

A 'Notes' section reports Jayaprakash Narayan's election as Honorary Chairman of the Congress for Cultural Freedom alongside Bertrand Russell and Jacques Maritain, and a Soviet circus defector's eyewitness testimony of Russian military participation in the Korean War.

Reviews cover M. A. Venkata Rao on Nicolai Hartmann's Ethics, and a Hague brochure on 'Law in Communist China' based on Father Andre Bonnichon's testimony describing a system where arrest itself is treated as proof of guilt.
Four Bombay I.C.C.F. members' letter protests the government's handling of the Bombay/Samyukta Maharashtra dispute; the editor replies defending the journal's neutrality on the dispute's merits.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Two Thousand Five Hundred Years' marks the Buddha's 2500th anniversary, reading his rejection of external authority as a contrast to totalitarian states that mould the individual mind.

A 'Notes' section recounts the hostile British reception of Bulganin and Khrushchev's 1956 UK visit, reports the collapse of Singapore student emigration to Communist China after early arrivals discovered repression, and dismisses the Cominform's dissolution as a hollow gesture.
S. R. Tikekar's 'Copyright Bill: Author's Viewpoint' criticises the new Bill for halving the copyright term to 25 years and vesting commissioned works' copyright in employers rather than authors.

'The End Of Equality In U.S.S.R.' cites Mikoyan's admission of a 62-to-1 income disparity between scientists and average Soviet workers to argue regulated capitalism has achieved more equality than Soviet-style planning.
Nabakishore Das's 'Prospects Of Democracy In India' warns that caste hierarchy and illiteracy, documented via 1951 Census figures, threaten Indian democracy absent a genuine opposition party.

A review of the symposium Why I Oppose Communism traces Minoo Masani's contribution recounting disillusionment with the USSR after the 1936 Purges, alongside M. A. Venkata Rao's review of Bertrand Russell's Human Society In Ethics And Politics.
A reader's letter cites Raymond Garthoff's How Russia Makes War to add further evidence of Soviet military pay disparities between privates and generals.

V. B. Karnik's 'Verdict On China' reports an international Brussels commission's findings, corroborated by 89 released Catholic missionaries, that forced labour in Communist China is economically embedded and 'reform through labour' constitutes 'a true concentrationary system.'

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Neogy Upsets The Apple Cart' details Planning Commission member K. C. Neogy's dissent, alongside B. R. Shenoy and C. N. Vakil, warning that deficit financing near Rs. 1200 crores would generate serious inflation.

A profile of visiting American novelist James T. Farrell situates him in the naturalist tradition of Dreiser and Sinclair Lewis, noting his refusal to let Marxism dictate his individual judgment despite earlier Trotskyite associations.
'Operation Lullaby' analyses the CPI's Fourth Congress at Palghat as mirroring 1930s Popular Front tactics, warning of growing Congress tolerance toward the CPI as a legitimate opposition.

V.B.K.'s review of Alwin H. Scaff's The Philippine Answer to Communism recounts President Magsaysay's 'all-out force and all-out friendship' defeat of the Huk rebellion via the EDCOR resettlement programme.
A correspondent's report on an I.C.C.F. seminar in Poona covers Maharashtra's casteism and liberal heritage, with M. R. Masani forcefully countering claims that liberalism was 'dead and gone.'

A four-page supplement, 'Social Democrats In Communist Jails,' reproduces a letter to Khrushchev and Bulganin from international socialist leaders including Julius Braunthal, Norman Thomas and A. Philip Randolph, demanding release of over 350 imprisoned socialists and trade unionists across the USSR and Eastern Europe.

The unsigned editorial 'Only A Handful' rebuts Nehru's claim that only a 'handful' of critics disagree with non-alignment, arguing Indian foreign policy applies a double standard by staying silent on Soviet purges while condemning Western colonialism.

A 'Notes' section reports renewed persecution of Milovan Djilas despite Tito's Moscow rapprochement, profiles new Soviet Foreign Minister Dmitri Shepilov's earlier letter instructing Indian communists to avoid embarrassing Indo-Soviet diplomacy, and covers U Nu's surprise resignation in Burma.

G. S. Bhargava's 'The Double Standard In Action,' abridged from The New Leader, diagnoses Indian intellectuals' selective outrage -- fury at the Rosenberg executions but silence on Beria's execution -- and links Nehru's Soviet tilt to managing domestic communists.

Ida Dhami's 'Whither Algeria?' surveys the Algerian independence crisis, noting nine million indigenous Algerians against roughly one million French colons, and warns of Soviet or Egyptian exploitation if no settlement is reached.

Adam Adil's 'Can Socialists & Communists Cooperate?' examines talks between Jayaprakash Narayan, Asoka Mehta and CPI's Ajoy Ghosh, citing the 1948 Czechoslovak coup and the deaths of Jan Masaryk and President Benes as the definitive warning against united fronts with communists.

A letter from S. R. Mohan Das corrects an earlier note on the INTUC's stance on the right to strike, and I.C.C.F. News reports James T. Farrell's Bombay and Delhi visit, including a long interview with the Prime Minister.
'With Many Voices' quotes Ajoy Kumar Ghosh admitting the 'cult of personality' around Nehru is well developed in India, alongside Eisenhower calling communism 'a gigantic failure.'

V. B. Karnik's 'The Indictment Of Stalin' surveys global reaction to Khrushchev's secret speech, arguing the condemnation is self-serving since it excuses earlier purges of Trotsky and Bukharin and offers no pledge of civil liberties or habeas corpus.

K. K. Sinha's 'The Guilty Men And Their System' argues Stalin's crimes were the structural product of Leninist party dictatorship, predicting reverence will simply transfer to a new 'Great Pupil of Lenin.'

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'The Poznan Portent' treats the June 1956 Polish workers' revolt as proof of Soviet planning's failure, tracing the unrest to bread shortages, suppressed nationalism, and the retention of roughly two million Poles in Soviet labour camps.

Solidarity statements from European intellectuals including Albert Camus, Karl Jaspers, Arthur Koestler and Ignazio Silone, and from prominent Indians including Sophia Wadia and B. R. Shenoy, demand an end to repression of the Poznan workers' leaders.

A 'Notes' section criticises Congress President U. N. Dhebar's remark equating loyalty to Nehru with not opposing his wishes, links it to C. D. Deshmukh's resignation speech, and endorses C. Rajagopalachari's warning about an uncritically adulatory Indian press.

'With Many Voices' quotes K. M. Munshi lamenting that no university teaches Gandhi's or Ramakrishna's philosophy, and Frank Moraes warning Soviet strategy is shifting from coexistence to popular fronts.

V. B. Karnik's 'Strange If True' argues that even limited electoral 'adjustments' between the PSP and Communist Party would inevitably escalate into a united front, invoking the 1930s Congress Socialist Party precedent and Burma's AFPFL experience as cautionary parallels.

A 'Notes' section reports Chinese incursion into Burmese territory, criticises the Madhya Pradesh Niyogi Committee report on Christian missionaries as 'reckless,' and reveals C. D. Deshmukh's resignation disclosures on unconstitutional cabinet decision-making over Bombay's reorganisation.

An unsigned report traces Indonesia's post-election cabinet formation, in which the Communist Party (P.K.I.) became Asia's second-largest despite ultimately being excluded from the resulting government.

M. A. Venkata Rao's piece on the planned Asian Writers' Conference questions whether a unified 'Asian Mind' exists, arguing the Moscow-aligned sponsors intend the Delhi conference as a communist 'Front' or 'communication belt.'

Eugene Lyons's 'An Open Letter To A Fellow-Traveller,' addressed to novelist Howard Fast, presses him to recognise his response to Khrushchev's revelations as 'a cry for help' rather than a genuine break from communism.
M. A. Venkata Rao reviews Klaus Mehnert's Stalin versus Marx, concluding Soviet ideology's shift to national conservatism amounts to 'a new Fascism -- a strange meeting of extremes.'
'With Many Voices' quotes Nehru saying no one in a communist country can raise their head against Party decisions, and K.P.S. Menon noting India has 'followed your (Soviet) example' economically.

An exclusive interview has Jayaprakash Narayan deny any ideological sympathy for the CPI while defending a narrowly tactical electoral seat-adjustment as a safeguard against near one-party Congress rule, explicitly ruling out any united front.

'Fresh Light On Communist Machinations' describes the Democratic Research Service's disclosure of secret CPI Fourth Congress documents revealing internal 'frustration and cynicism' and continued fealty to Moscow even after de-Stalinisation.

V. B. Karnik's 'The Danger To Democracy' welcomes JP's clarification but criticises his suggestion that communists be allowed to govern a state democratically, since once in power they entrench themselves and end free elections.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Behind U Nu's Resignation' attributes the Burmese leader's surprise retirement to disillusionment with Soviet and Chinese embassy interference rather than his stated reason of party purification.

A translated Soviet article by Yu. P. Nasenko, reproduced as evidence of Moscow's own analysis, dismisses Indian socialists' 'democratic socialism' as cover for hostility to Marxism and alleges American funding of the 1951-52 Socialist election campaign.

'A Misleading Report' criticises an Indian delegation's report on Chinese agricultural collectivisation for taking propaganda at face value while its own text admits middle and upper farmers were eliminated 'through terror and coercion.'

The 'Notes' section covers a communal riot linked to a republished book, film censorship of the American documentary 'With These Hands,' and the Punjab Special Powers Press Act's pre-censorship provisions.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Homage To Hungary' argues the Hungarian uprising went further than Poland's protests by rejecting the entire one-party communist system, recounting Soviet suppression of Budapest demonstrators and appeals to Nehru from Ference Nagy and Western intellectuals.

V. B. Karnik's 'Asian Socialist Conference' argues Asian socialists can pursue industrialisation without sacrificing civil liberties, rejecting the claim that totalitarian methods are necessary, and citing Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia as counterexamples that never produced democratic societies.

An unsigned 'Soviet Economy And Its Problems' marshals Pravda, Khrushchev, Bulganin and Mikoyan's own admissions of falling livestock numbers, chronic housing shortages and consumer-goods scarcity to indict Soviet central planning.

Adam Adil's 'Situation In South Africa' documents the forced removal of over 100,000 non-whites, including 22,000 Indians, from Johannesburg under the Group Areas Act, with losses to Indian traders estimated at over £22 million.

A 'Notes' section reads the Sino-Nepal Treaty as extending Chinese influence at India's expense and criticises Nehru for supporting a restrictive new Punjab press bill despite his own democratic history.
Reviews cover Walter Laqueur's Communism and Nationalism in the Middle East and the anthology From Darkness to Light, drawing on the Upanishads, the Gita and modern Indian thinkers.

A reader's letter signed 'Politicus' argues India's Single Member Constituency system risks squeezing out moderate parties, leaving only Congress and the Communist Party viable and risking 'hanging democracy by its own rope.'

The unsigned editorial 'D.R.S. Answers The P.M.' rebuts Nehru's Parliamentary charge that the Democratic Research Service and I.C.C.F. are communist-front organisations, detailing the DRS's 1950 founding under Sardar Patel's blessing and reproducing Jayaprakash Narayan's public defence of its record.

'India And Hungary' criticises the Government's slow, equivocal response to Soviet intervention in Hungary, singling out V. K. Krishna Menon's UN vote alongside the Soviet bloc as damaging India's moral standing.

Soetan Sjarir, former Prime Minister of Indonesia, delivers 'Russian War Against Hungary' at a Bombay public meeting, condemning the Soviet crackdown as classical imperialism and urging Asian vigilance against 'Red imperialism.'
An unsigned report describes the formation of the Indian Committee for Solidarity with Hungary under Jayaprakash Narayan's presidency, who demands Krishna Menon's recall from the UN.

'A Call For Healthy Insight,' a joint statement by writers including Ram Singh and Sudhindranath Datta, argues India's intelligentsia refuses on ideological grounds to recognise Soviet imperialism even while vigilantly opposing Western colonialism.

A letter signed 'T.M.' argues Nehru's shift toward satyagraha rhetoric on Hungary is more authentic than invoking Panchshila, likening the latter's non-interference logic to Cain's 'Am I my brother's keeper' evasion.

V. B. Karnik's 'The Beginning Of The End' surveys the Soviet crushing of the Hungarian revolution, quoting Milovan Djilas's judgment that it may mark 'the beginning of the end of Communism generally,' and criticises the free world's failure to back Imre Nagy's appeal.

A 'Notes' section reports Soviet student unrest in Moscow and Leningrad as a ripple effect of Hungary, Bombay Education Minister Shantilal Shah's opposition to state control of the film industry, and a tribute to the recently deceased B. R. Ambedkar.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Copyright Bill' reports the Joint Select Committee's restoration of the copyright term to fifty years, while criticising the Bill's vesting of commissioned works' copyright in commissioning parties rather than authors.

'Mr. Djilas And Marshal Tito' reports Djilas's secret trial and three-year sentence for his New Leader article on Hungary, with international protest from the American Committee for Cultural Freedom and Tito's own biographer Vladimir Dedijer.

'Saadi' defends the Democratic Research Service against Nehru's charge of being 'propagandist rather than a search for truth,' contrasting Nehru's own eulogy of Stalin with the DRS's five-year record of warnings later vindicated.

A correspondent's report on the Delhi Asian Writers' Conference describes it as nearly wrecked by communist-versus-anti-communist tensions, with Rajaji arguing art's purpose is to create beauty, not propaganda.

'Echoes Of The Hungarian Revolution' compiles international statements, including Denis de Rougemont's refusal to normalise relations with anyone who 'justifies' Budapest and Norman Thomas's criticism of Krishna Menon's UN vote.
Francois Bondy's first-person 'A Moment In Budapest' recounts conversations with Hungarian writers, including Julius Hay and Tibor Dery, on the eve of the Soviet crackdown.

V. B. Karnik's editorial 'General Election' predicts India's 1957 poll will change little given popular indifference and hero-worship, warning fifteen unbroken years of Congress rule risks strengthening totalitarian tendencies within a nominally democratic system.

A 'Notes' section reports apartheid crackdowns in South Africa under the Group Areas and Suppression of Communism Acts, and protests the Preventive Detention Act arrests of about twenty-five Praja Socialist workers in Ahmedabad.

Manes Sperber's 'The West Has Lost The Right To Weep,' reprinted from The New Leader, delivers a bitter indictment of Western passivity during the Hungarian revolution, invoking Rosa Luxemburg's thesis on the spontaneity of the masses.

'Saadi''s essay '"We Are All Stalinists"' dissects Khrushchev's continued praise of Stalin as a 'model communist,' reporting a secret Comintern-successor directive instructing all Communist Parties to defend Soviet action in Hungary.
An international cable to Tito, signed by figures including T. S. Eliot, Albert Camus and Indians Jayaprakash Narayan, M. R. Masani and B. R. Shenoy, demands Milovan Djilas's release.
A. B. Shah reports on a Karachi seminar on 'Religion and Freedom,' where participants debated whether Islam or any religion can guarantee individual political and cultural freedom.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Officialising The Cooperatives?' opposes Minister K. D. Malaviya's call to officialise cooperatives, citing comparative evidence that forced collectivisation nowhere raised agricultural output above pre-revolution levels.

V. B. Karnik's 'Back To Stalinism?' argues Soviet de-Stalinisation was never genuine liberalisation but a tactical retreat forced by near-collapse of control after Hungary and Poland, quoting Khrushchev's own admission that he does 'not separate Stalinism and Stalin from Communism.'

G. F. Hudson's 'The Paradox Of Jawaharlal Nehru,' condensed from Commentary, dissects a 'double standard' in Nehru's foreign policy -- harsh on Suez, muted on Hungary -- while still affirming Nehru's 'basic devotion to liberal principles.'

'The Truth About Poland' extensively quotes Gomulka's October 1956 Central Committee report admitting the Six Year Plan's failure and attributing the Poznan riots to genuine grievances rather than foreign incitement.

Extracts from Oscar Lange's Zycie Gospodarcze article, introduced as the economist who advised Mahalanobis on India's Second Plan, detail Poland's 'disintegration of the national economy' and propose a nine-point emergency programme including 'further democratization.'

B. K. Desai reviews Peter Fryer's Hungarian Tragedy, praising Fryer's firsthand account of 'three and a half days of freedom' while faulting his continued loyalty to a Communist Party he intends to 'reform from within.'
Franklin A. Lindsay's counterfactual 'What Might Have Happened In Hungary,' from Free Spirit, imagines a UN Observation Commission and decisive Western intervention averting the Soviet crackdown.
A 'Notes' section welcomes Indian government moves against communist-front organisations, university autonomy calls from John Matthai and Vinoba Bhave, and marks the birth of the Republic of Ghana.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Kerala: The Cockpit' assesses the CPI's Kerala election victory, winning 60 of 126 seats, as reflecting disgust with Congress and PSP misgovernment rather than ideological conversion, warning of the psychological danger of lending communism respectability.

A 'Notes' section reports renewed Soviet-Yugoslav tension, alleges communist infiltration of the AICC's Economic Review, and describes a Bulgarian youth organ's attack on Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah as evidence of a coordinated communist campaign against new states.

Ida Dhami's 'Signor Nenni's Change Of Heart' reports Italian socialist leader Pietro Nenni's break from a decade-long communist alliance following Khrushchev's revelations and the Hungarian and Poznan uprisings.

'Saadi''s survey of student discontent behind the Iron Curtain documents unrest in East Germany, Hungary, Poland and the USSR, concluding that Marxism and Communism are 'obviously losing their appeal to the Soviet students and intelligentsia.'

Raja Kulkarni surveys parliamentary democracy's fragile state across Asia -- Sukarno's 'Guided Democracy' proposal in Indonesia, Thailand's contested elections, Burma's Karen insurgency -- and frames Kerala's communist government as the decisive test case for the Indian constitutional framework.

B. K. Desai reviews Bertram D. Wolfe's Six Keys to the Soviet System and Khrushchev and Stalin's Ghost, summarising Wolfe's argument that the real twentieth-century question is 'total state or limited state' and that Khrushchev's speech selectively omitted the Hitler-Stalin pact and Katyn.
Short obituaries mourn Philippine President Ramon Magsaysay, credited with defeating the Huk insurgency through land reform, and former Bombay Chief Minister B. G. Kher.

V. B. Karnik's 'The Elections And After' reviews the 1957 general elections, attributing the CPI's stronger showing -- capturing Kerala and gaining seats in Bengal -- not to communist strength but to the 'confused, supine and divided' state of India's democratic forces.

An extract from Wolfgang Harich's smuggled memorandum, 'Testament Of A Party Rebel,' describes an East German reformist faction seeking to shed the party's residual Stalinism and calling for elections with real choice, written shortly before his arrest and ten-year sentence for treason.

M. A. Venkata Rao praises the Patel-Rana Dissenting Note on Chinese 'agricultural cooperatives,' which argues Chinese collectives strip peasants of proprietorship through manufactured 'voluntary' accession following prior land-reform terror.

Writing as 'Ekalavya,' an essay on communist 'mis-education' documents Soviet-bloc textbooks' indoctrination of hatred toward 'Anglo-American imperialists' and warns the same methods could reach Kerala's newly communist-run schools.
A 'Notes' section reports Aneurin Bevan's candid criticism of Soviet and Chinese collectivisation's countryside discontent and a wave of British Communist Party resignations after Hungary and Poland.
'With Many Voices' closes with a satirical mock dinner-invitation from A. K. Gopalan's Kerala communist government to leading industrialists, 'and Harakiri soon thereafter.'

V. B. Karnik's 'Party, Government And The People' critiques Nehru's claim that India occupies a middle position between Communist party-state fusion and Western parliamentary democracy, warning that identifying government with Congress would be 'a step in the direction of totalitarianism.'

Leszek Kolakowski's 'What Is Socialism?,' smuggled from the banned Polish paper Po Prostu, builds a long ironic catalogue of what socialism is 'not' -- a police state, a system with more spies than nurses -- before its deliberately anticlimactic close, 'socialism is a good thing.'

A 'Notes' section describes new Second Plan taxation and deficit financing, the USSR's 1957 decree freezing repayment of state bonds as a de facto default, and the arrests of Indonesian writers Takdir Alisjahbana and Mochtar Lubis without charges.
M. A. Venkata Rao reviews Kwame Nkrumah's autobiography Ghana on the occasion of Ghanaian independence, describing his thought as 'an amalgam of Marxist specialism and Mazzinian nationalism.'

Hans Edward Teglers's interview with Yugoslav politician Vladimir Dedijer has him argue Marx today would write Das Kapital against Soviet exploitation of its own people, concluding the Soviet experiment's lesson is 'how not to do it.'

C.C.F. News reports plans for a 1959 East-West Music Festival in Tokyo and reiterates protests over the Indonesian writers' arrests, while an article on Indian cooperative farming warns against following the Chinese collectivisation model.

V. B. Karnik's 'Mao's Flowers And Weeds' analyses Mao's 'Hundred Flowers' speech, noting Mao's own admission that his security forces liquidated 800,000 people between 1949 and 1954, and reads the slogan as freedom only 'with leadership.'

A 'Notes' section condemns the paralysis of French policy after 34 months of war in Algeria and praises the UN Investigating Committee's report establishing that Soviet intervention in Hungary was 'massive armed intervention' unrequested by the Hungarian government.

Adam Adil's two-part 'Philosophy Of Freedom' surveys the idea of liberty from Plato through Locke and Mill, arguing economic freedom should accompany but not be a precondition of political freedom, quoting Gaitskell's rejection of that doctrine as 'dangerous nonsense.'

J. H. Oldenbroek's message marks the fourth anniversary of the 1953 East German workers' revolt, recounting how 274 cities rose against imposed pay differentials and pervasive surveillance before Soviet tanks crushed the uprising.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Educational Policies In Kerala' warns that the communist government's proposed textbook nationalisation risks rewriting history along Marxist-Leninist lines and disparaging figures like Shivaji as 'communal.'

A reprinted correspondence between Soviet critic Ivan Anissimov and Ignazio Silone ends with Silone declaring 'a dialogue between us is impossible' given Soviet censorship, after pressing Anissimov on the unresolved death of Maxim Gorky and disappeared writers.

V. B. Karnik's 'Whither Bhoodan?' questions whether the Bhoodan movement's evolution into Gramdan, whole-village land gifts, risks drifting toward Soviet-style collectivisation, citing Vinoba Bhave's remark that he might accept 'the communist way' if non-violence fails.

A 'Notes' section rebuts a libel republished by Blitz alleging foreign funding of the Democratic Research Service and M. R. Masani, and reports growing complaints of lawlessness under Kerala's communist ministry led by E. M. S. Namboodiripad.

The United Nations Special Committee's report on Hungary, reprinted in full, concludes the 1956 uprising was a spontaneous national revolt, not fomented by Western or reactionary forces, and finds evidence Soviet troop movements began before the Hungarian government's request.
Paul Ignotus's firsthand account, 'The Hungarian Revolution,' recalls Hungarian writers' central role in the uprising and catalogues fellow writers arrested, imprisoned or disappeared afterward.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'On The Chinese Road!' argues India's cooperative-farming push mirrors Communist China's collectivisation, which transferred control of the harvest from peasant to state, contrasting this with Denmark's ownership-preserving cooperative model.

A statement by Kerala's Private Schools' Rights' Defense Committee opposes the communist government's plan to nationalise 'badly run' private schools, comparing the approach to Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy.

A letter from Rev. T. Mascarenhas rebuts Venkata Rao's suggested equivalence between Catholic school doctrine and communist indoctrination, defending Catholic schools' constitutional right to operate without compelling outsiders.

Adam Adil's 'Ten Years Of Freedom' takes stock of a decade of Indian independence, warning against the personality cult fostered by a Films Division documentary on Nehru and against the drift toward 'statism' via cooperative-farming proposals he calls disguised collectivisation.

A 'Notes' section welcomes the averted post-and-telegraph strike but criticises the Essential Services Maintenance Bill, and reports K. M. Munshi's warning that proposed tax tribunals represent totalitarianism entering with 'padded feet.'

Excerpts from Milovan Djilas's smuggled manuscript The New Class contrast bourgeois revolutions' gains in civil rights with communist revolutions' gains accruing only to the ruling bureaucracy, and document 20,000 cases of 'socialist property' theft in Yugoslavia in 1954.

V. N. Rudin's 'The Split In The Kremlin?' analyses Khrushchev's July 1957 purge of the Molotov-Malenkov-Kaganovich faction, concluding power has shifted to the 318-member Central Committee, diluting central Soviet authority.
R. S. Panday marks Malaya's independence on 31 August 1957, crediting British rule with infrastructure and stability while noting the economy's dependence on rubber and tin.
A Democratic Research Service discussion on the Kerala Education Bill warns it could enable 'nationalisation of education from the back-door' and communist indoctrination.

V. B. Karnik reviews three books on the Hungarian Revolution -- Michener's The Bridge At Andau, Mikes's The Hungarian Revolution, and Barber's A Handful Of Ashes -- quoting a passage accusing Nehru of moral cowardice for his silence during the crisis.

Writing as 'Jupiter,' an essay titled '"Kerala Communists Are Different..."' argues the claim is a deliberately cultivated Communist strategy rather than fact, since the CPI has mirrored every twist of Soviet policy including de-Stalinisation and Hungary.

James Critchlow's 'Ilya Ehrenburg Rebels' describes Ehrenburg's essay 'Lessons of Stendhal' as the strongest public challenge to Communist cultural dictatorship since Stalin's rise, defending dissident writer Vladimir Dudintsev.

V. B. Karnik's 'Our Vote On Hungary' condemns India's UN abstention on the Hungary resolution, rejecting the government's comparison to Suez since England and France, unlike the USSR, complied with UN resolutions.

Adam Adil's 'Our Language Problem' surveys the Hindi-versus-English dispute following the Official Language Commission's report, noting fifty MPs sought a 25-year postponement and quoting Rajagopalachari's proposal that both languages serve jointly.

A 'Notes' section welcomes an apparent government retreat from Chinese-style collectivisation toward voluntary 'service cooperatives,' and reports B. R. Shenoy's and K. M. Munshi's warnings at a Bombay welfare-state symposium against 'equivocal slogans' concealing Marxian dogma.

Extracts from Kodanda Rao's press statement dispute the Official Language Commission majority's characterisation of English as 'foreign,' arguing bilingualism serves the public better than the majority's proposed trilingualism.
Two readers' letters debate the West German election's implications for reunification and press Adam Adil to name which Indian language should replace English if not Hindi.
